traveler: Saint Eustace (Placidus, Eustathios), with Theopista, Agapius and Theopistus
title: The Stag That Hunted the Hunter: Placidus, the Bronze Bull, and Six Hundred Years to the First Document
years: c. 98-118 (legendary); cult attested from the 5th-8th centuries
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rome, the house by the plane tree
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Trajan's reign (98-117) is attested history; the man Placidus is not. No second-century inscription, historian, or administrative record names him. The identification of this block as his house site is a Roman church tradition, first recorded centuries after the legend's own date, and the byname 'in platana' is the only thread holding it.
stops.campa: A plane tree stands in the low ground between the Pantheon and the bend of the Tiber, and Roman church tradition puts the house of Placidus beneath it. He is rich, married, the father of two boys, a soldier of high rank. He gives alms to the poor of the city out of ordinary piety and has never heard the name of Christ. No inscription on this block names him. What stands here is a church that took the byname in platana from the tree, and a story working backward from the church to the man it needs to have lived in it.
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, 'The Life of S. Eustace'
suggested_refs: Piazza di Sant'Eustachio, Rome, and the church byname 'in platana'

stops.name: Rome, Trajan's Forum: the rank the legend gives him
stops.date_confidence: the reign is attested; the rank is an anachronism. The Latin tradition calls Placidus magister militum, an office created under Constantine in the fourth century and nonexistent under Trajan. The Greek Passio uses stratelates, which at least could have been spoken. Treat the Latin title as a later hagiographic gloss, not a Trajanic command.
stops.campa: Trajan holds the empire from 98 and the column that will carry his Dacian wars up its spiral is not yet cut. Into this court the legend inserts Placidus, commander of the emperor's armies, the man the emperor cannot do without. The Latin tradition calls him magister militum. The Greek calls him stratelates. Only the Greek word could have been spoken in this forum: the Latin office will not be invented for two hundred years, under Constantine. The story keeps the general and dresses him in the wrong century's uniform.
suggested_refs: Trajan's Forum and Column, Rome; the Notitia Dignitatum for the actual date of the magister militum

stops.name: Monte Guadagnolo, the crucifix between the antlers
stops.date_confidence: legendary event, real place. The Santuario della Mentorella at 41.9214/12.9364 is attested from the sixth century as Benedictine and then Subiaco property; an earlier draft of this dossier used 41.8964/12.9107, which is empty hillside 3.4 km southwest and wrong. Its identification as the exact vision site is tradition only.
stops.campa: The hunt runs east out of Rome into the hills between Tivoli and Palestrina, and on the shoulder of Monte Guadagnolo, a thousand metres up, the stag turns and stands. Between its antlers is a crucifix brighter than the sun, and the beast speaks with the voice of the man on the cross. Placidus comes off his horse onto the ground. A sanctuary holds this rock, given to Benedictines in the sixth century and kept by Subiaco until the fifteenth, and it tells travellers this is the place. The rock is a great deal older than the claim.
stops.quote: Placidus, wherefore followest me hither? I am appeared to thee in this beast for the grace of thee. I am Jesu Christ, whom thou honourest ignorantly, thy alms be ascended up tofore me, and therefore I come hither so that by this hart that thou huntest I may hunt thee.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. William Caxton, ed. F. S. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (London: J. M. Dent, 1900), 'The Life of S. Eustace', p. 84
suggested_refs: The Santuario della Mentorella on Monte Guadagnolo, 1,018 m, Capranica Prenestina

stops.name: Monte Guadagnolo, the voice names itself
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The dialogue is given verbatim only in the Passio and its descendants; the Caxton wording quoted here is a fifteenth-century English rendering of a thirteenth-century Latin compilation of a Greek text of the fifth to seventh centuries.
stops.campa: Placidus, on the ground, asks the voice to say again what it has said, and it does. What comes back is a creed rather than a summons: maker of heaven and earth, divider of light from darkness, founder of time and days and hours, shaper of men out of the slime, crucified and buried and risen the third day. Placidus answers that he believes. He is sent down the mountain to the bishop of the city to be washed and told to come back up here afterward. Then he asks whether he is to keep this from his wife.
stops.quote: I am Jesu Christ that formed heaven and earth, which made the light to increase, and divided it from darkness, and established time, days, and hours. Which formed men of the slime of the earth, which appeared on earth in flesh for the health of the lineage human, which was crucified, dead, buried, and arose the third day.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, pp. 84-85
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: The Caxton-Ellis Temple Classics text of the Life of S. Eustace, archive.org identifier TheGoldenLegendV6

stops.name: Rome, the bishop's font
stops.date_confidence: legendary, and the site is a placeholder. The Passio names no church and no baptistery, only 'the bishop of the city'; the coordinate repeats the traditional house site because the text offers nothing else. The wife is unnamed before baptism in the Caxton text, which gives her new name as Theospis; other traditions call her Tatiana and Theopista.
stops.campa: He rides home and finds his wife already holding the thing he came to tell her. She has had the vision the same night and has been told that tomorrow she and her husband and their sons will come to Christ. They go to the bishop of Rome together, at night. Placidus is baptised Eustace, his wife takes the name Theopista, the boys become Agapius and Theopistus. Four Roman names go under the water and four Greek ones come out, and the family that will be taken apart piece by piece is assembled here in a single hour.
stops.quote: My Lord! ... I saw him this night that is passed, and he said to me: To-morn thou, thy husband, and thy sons, shall come to me. And now I know that it was Christ.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, p. 85; the words of Eustace's wife, reporting her own vision the same night
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: The names Eustathios, Theopiste, Agapios and Theopistos as they stand in the Byzantine synaxarion

stops.name: Monte Guadagnolo, the warning of Job
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The second-vision episode exists only in the literary Passio. The Job parallel is not a later reader's inference: philologists point to it as the borrowed template, and the text itself makes the comparison out loud.
stops.campa: He climbs back to the mountain as instructed and the voice is waiting with terms. He has trodden the devil under his foot, and the devil is armed against him for it. His faith must now appear, and it will appear by suffering. Eustace does not bargain. He asks that the temptation come at once and that he be given the patience to hold under it. He is told to be constant, that grace will keep the souls of his household. The Book of Job is the pattern the legend hands him openly, in advance, with the ending kept back.
stops.quote: Eustace, thou that art blessed, which hast taken the washing of grace, for now thou hast surmounted the devil, which had deceived thee, and trodden him under foot, now thy faith shall appear. The devil now, because thou hast forsaken him, is armed cruelly against thee, and it behoveth thee to suffer many things and pains.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, pp. 85-86
sources: Comparative literary-hagiographic scholarship on the Placidus legend type, summarized at en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint Eustace'
suggested_refs: The Book of Job as the acknowledged template of the Placidus narrative type

stops.name: Rome, the plague in the stables and the robbers at the door
stops.date_confidence: legendary; no attested location beyond the traditional house site, and no attested date at all. The month and day are defaults, not evidence.
stops.campa: The trial begins the way the Book of Job begins. A pestilence takes the servants of the household and then the horses and the cattle, in a stroke, without warning. What the plague leaves, thieves carry out of the house by night. Eustace, who commanded armies out of this door, will not be seen poor in the city where he was rich. He gathers Theopista and the two boys in the dark and walks out of Rome, leaving the name Placidus behind him with the property. The legend does not say who is left to notice that he has gone.
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: Job 1:13-19, the pattern of the losses in a single stroke

stops.name: Ostia, the ship for Egypt
stops.date_confidence: inference, not attestation. The Golden Legend names no port of departure. Ostia is supplied here as the standard Rome-to-Egypt embarkation of the period; the text supports Egypt as the destination and nothing else about the route.
stops.campa: Rome's port stands at the Tiber mouth, sixteen miles from the city, and every grain ship out of Egypt ends here. The family takes passage the other way, four people with no baggage buying a crossing they cannot pay for. The Golden Legend names neither the port nor the captain and gives no destination past Egypt; Ostia is supplied by the shipping lanes and not by the text. From here the story leaves any ground a map can check and enters a geography made of one sea, one river, and a village nobody has ever found.
sources: inference from Roman shipping routes; not named in the source text
suggested_refs: The harbour basins of Ostia and Portus, the Rome end of the Alexandrian grain run

stops.name: Alexandria, the master takes the wife
stops.date_confidence: legendary event, supplied coordinate. No Egyptian port is named in the legend. Alexandria is the empire's principal harbour on this coast and is used as the likeliest landfall; the pin is at the Pharos promontory, marked in the modern landscape by the Qaitbay Citadel, which postdates the legend by more than a millennium.
stops.campa: The crossing ends and the fare comes due. The shipmaster, seeing the passenger has nothing, takes the woman in payment and puts the man and the boys ashore. Eustace turns to his sons on the sand and says the plainest sentence in the whole legend. Alexandria is the great harbour of this coast and the only plausible landfall, but the text names no harbour at all: the pin marks the likeliest door into Egypt, not an attested one. Theopista goes out of the story here and stays out of it for fifteen years.
stops.quote: Alas! woe am I for you, for your mother is delivered to a strange husband.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, p. 87
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: The Pharos promontory at Alexandria, ancient harbour of the Egyptian grain fleet

stops.name: The Delta, the lion and the wolf
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the river is unnamed in every surviving version. The Delta coordinate is illustrative and asserts nothing. Note the correction: the name Hydaspes belongs to the later battle episode, not to this crossing. Earlier summaries that attach Alexander's river to the loss of the sons misplace it.
stops.campa: A river lies across the road and it is too deep to carry both boys at once. He takes the elder over, sets him down, and goes back into the water for the younger. Midstream he turns and sees a lion take the child on the far bank and a wolf take the child behind him, each carried off into the country in opposite directions. He stands in the river with nothing in his arms. The river is unnamed in every surviving version, and the Delta point here is a placeholder for a place the sources decline to give.
stops.quote: Alas! woe is me! for tofore this mishap I shone in great wealth like a tree, but now I am naked of all things... O good Lord, give thou rest to my tribulations, and keep thou so my mouth that mine heart decline not into words of malice, and be cast from thy visage.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, pp. 87-88
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint Eustace' (on the Hydaspes and the battle, not the crossing)
suggested_refs: The river-crossing panel in the Chartres Eustace window, baie 43

stops.name: The Delta, the shepherds and the plowmen
stops.date_confidence: legendary; no village is named and no location can be fixed. Coordinate repeated from the crossing as a placeholder.
stops.campa: Shepherds working the far bank see the wolf and drive it off, and it puts the child down unhurt. Plowmen with dogs see the lion and shout it down, and it sets the other child on the ground and goes. The two boys are taken into two households in the same district, raised as strangers to each other, not knowing they are brothers. Their father is a mile downriver and knows none of it. The legend keeps this from him for fifteen years and tells the reader at once, which is the machinery of the whole tale running in the open.
suggested_refs: The 'Man Tried by Fate' narrative type, of which this is the defining episode

stops.name: Badioson, the field-watchman
stops.date_confidence: the village is a stated gap. The Greek text gives Badioson (Badiosōn); the Latin copies garble it to Badissus and Badesia. English Wikipedia: 'The village of Badioson where Eustace retires after the loss of his family is unknown.' The coordinate here is a Delta placeholder and locates nothing.
stops.campa: He comes to a village the Greek text calls Badioson and hires himself out to watch its fields. The wage is bread. He does the work fifteen years without moving and without being known, a Roman general standing in a crop at night keeping birds and thieves off another man's harvest. Badioson has never been matched to any place on the earth, and the Latin copies, which write Badissus and Badesia, are no help. The coordinate here marks the Delta and nothing narrower. The village is a gap and is left as one.
suggested_refs: Badioson (Βαδιοσών) in the Greek Passio, BHG 641

stops.name: Rome, Antiochus and Acacius are sent out
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Trajan's court is historical; the search mission is not. No campaign, no frontier crisis, and no officers of these names appear in any second-century source for Trajan's command.
stops.campa: Barbarians press the frontier and the emperor finds he has no general fit for them. Trajan remembers Placidus, missing these fifteen years, and sends two officers, Antiochus and Acacius, to search the provinces of the world for one man. They carry a description and no address. The legend equips this search with an emperor, two named officers and a frontier in crisis. It leaves the historian nothing: no campaign, no dispatch, no name in any list of the commanders Trajan is known to have had.
suggested_refs: The prosopography of Trajan's senatorial commanders, in which no Placidus appears

stops.name: Badioson, the scar
stops.date_confidence: legendary; same unlocated village as the labour episode, same placeholder coordinate.
stops.campa: The two officers come through the village and lodge with the field-watchman without knowing him. He knows them at once and says nothing. They talk of the general they are sent to find, and then one of them sees on the labourer's body an old wound taken in a war they both remember, and fifteen years come apart in a moment. He is washed, dressed, given back his rank, and put on the road to Rome to raise an army. The recognition turns on a scar, which is the device that returns Odysseus to Ithaca, and the legend does not disguise the borrowing.
sources: Comparative scholarship on the Greco-Roman romance conventions borrowed by the Passio
suggested_refs: Odyssey XIX, the scar of Odysseus recognized by Eurycleia

stops.name: Egypt, the billet and the two soldiers
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the village on the line of march is unnamed and no fixed location survives in any source. Placeholder coordinate.
stops.campa: The new army marches through Egypt and Eustace billets two young soldiers near his own tent. He overhears them at night working out who they are. One tells of being carried off by a lion at a river when he was small and raised afterward by strangers; the other tells the same story with a wolf in it, and they understand they are brothers. Their commander, standing outside in the dark, understands more than they do. He has both sons back inside a single conversation he was never meant to hear.
suggested_refs: The recognition scenes of Greek romance, the structural parent of this episode

stops.name: Egypt, the poor woman's inn
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the inn is unnamed and unlocated. Placeholder coordinate. The Caxton text says the wife has been 'kept from all corruption' in the whole interval, which is the legend's own answer to the question the shipmaster's seizure raises.
stops.campa: The column halts at a poor inn kept by a woman who has held on to her life and her honour since the day a shipmaster took her off a beach. She listens to the officer talk, works out who he is, and asks him to tell her his first estate. Then she names Placidus, master of the knights, otherwise called Eustace, converted by the saviour of the world, tried in these particular ways, and says that she is his wife. Four people separated one at a time are in one room. The legend has spent fifteen years getting here.
stops.quote: Sir, I pray thee to tell of thy first estate, for I ween that thou art Placidus, master of the knights, which otherwise art called Eustace, whom the Saviour of the world hath converted, and hast suffered such temptation and such, and I that am thy wife was taken from thee in the sea, which nevertheless have been kept from all corruption.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, pp. 91-92
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: The reunion panel in the Chartres Eustace window, baie 43

stops.name: The Hydaspes, the battle Alexander already fought
stops.date_confidence: the river IS named in the Passio, and that is the point. English Wikipedia: 'the river Hydaspes where Eustace fights his victorious battle with the barbarians alludes to Alexander the Great and bears no relation to any historical conflict fought by emperor Trajan.' Correcting an earlier draft of this dossier, which called the battlefield unnamed. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from the Hydaspes stop in alexander.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Passio names the river of the victory: the Hydaspes, in the Punjab, where Alexander broke Porus and his elephants four hundred and forty years before this march. No Roman army under Trajan is within two thousand miles of it. The hagiographer wanted a battle that would sound like the greatest battle he knew and took Alexander's river whole. This is the flattest evidence in the dossier that the story is literature: a Roman general standing on a battlefield that belongs to Alexander and to nobody else.
sources: alexander.journey.json, stop 'Hydaspes, the king who asked to be treated as a king'
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Hydaspes, 326 BCE, and the Alexander Romance tradition that carried its name into hagiography

stops.name: Rome, the Forum: the triumph
stops.date_confidence: legendary. No triumphal route is named in the text; the Forum is supplied as the customary ground of Roman military honours. No Trajanic triumph of these years belongs to any Placidus in the record.
stops.campa: The army comes back victorious and the general comes back with a wife and two sons nobody knew he had. Rome honours him for the campaign and restores the standing he walked away from in the dark sixteen years earlier. The legend puts the family at the top of the arc here: everything lost, everything returned. In the Book of Job that would be the last page. It is not the last page. The Forum coordinate is supplied as the usual ground of such honours, since the text names neither route nor arch nor day.
suggested_refs: The Via Sacra and the Roman Forum, customary ground of a returning commander's honours

stops.name: Selinus in Cilicia, Trajan dies on the road
stops.date_confidence: attested. Trajan dies at Selinus in Cilicia, modern Gazipasa in Turkey, about 9 August 117. An earlier draft of this dossier placed his death at Rome with a coordinate near the Circus Maximus; that is fabricated and is withdrawn here. Hadrian is in Syria at the accession and does not enter Rome until 9 July 118.
stops.campa: Trajan dies on the Cilician coast at Selinus, on the road home from the east, and the succession passes to Hadrian, who is in Syria and will not see Rome for another eleven months. The legend hands Eustace over at this point from an emperor who wanted him to an emperor who will kill him, and never says where the first one died. The emperor of the martyrdom is the one solid historical object the story owns, and it did not choose him for his history.
suggested_refs: Selinus (Gazipasa), Cilicia, where Trajan died in August 117

stops.name: Rome, the Capitoline: the refusal
stops.date_confidence: legendary event, real hill. The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus stood here and is archaeologically attested; the refusal on its steps is in no record but the Passio. The year 118 is the commonly given date and is confirmed as the tradition, but it is not the first year of Hadrian's reign: he acceded about 9 August 117 and entered Rome on 9 July 118.
stops.campa: Hadrian, in Rome since July, orders sacrifice on the Capitol in thanksgiving for the victory, and the general who won it will not go up to the temple. Asked why, Eustace says the one sentence the whole legend has been built to arrive at: that he worships and sacrifices to Jesus Christ and serves no other. His wife says it after him and his two sons say it after her. The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus stood on this hill and has been dug up. The refusal on its steps exists in one text and nowhere else.
stops.quote: I adore and do sacrifice to our Lord Jesu Christ, and only serve him.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, p. 93
suggested_refs: The podium of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Capitoline Hill

stops.name: Rome, the Flavian Amphitheatre: the lion lies down
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the venue is supplied. Most retellings say only 'the amphitheatre'. The Colosseum is inserted here as the standard site for such a sentence in this city and is not independently confirmed for this legend.
stops.campa: The four are sent onto the sand and a lion is loosed on them. It crosses the arena, lowers its head, lies down at their feet, and will not touch them. The crowd is looking at a Roman general and his family standing unharmed in front of an animal starved for the purpose. The Golden Legend says amphitheatre and does not say which one; the Colosseum is supplied as the standard venue for a sentence of this kind. A lion took one of these boys out of a river once and did not eat him either.
suggested_refs: The Flavian Amphitheatre, standard venue of damnatio ad bestias at Rome

stops.name: Rome, the brazen ox
stops.date_confidence: legendary, and the sources contradict each other on the site. Some place the execution in the Forum area, others near the Capitol, others in an amphitheatre; the contradiction is recorded here and not resolved. The year is usually 118, but the Caxton text itself says 'about the year 120, calends of November', and some martyrologies give later dates still.
stops.campa: A bull of bronze is heated over a fire until it glows and the four are shut inside it. They pray, commend themselves, and die together. Three days after, the metal is opened and the bodies are found whole, not burned, not marked, and Christians carry them off and bury them in a place no source names. The sources disagree about where in Rome the bull stood: some say the Forum, some the Capitol, some the amphitheatre. The disagreement is left standing. The year is given as 118, and in Caxton's own text as about 120.
stops.quote: And then the saints prayed and commended them unto our Lord, and entered into the ox, and there yielded up their spirits unto Jesu Christ.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI, p. 93
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton, ed. Ellis, Temple Classics vol. VI (1900)
suggested_refs: The brazen bull of Phalaris, the older Greek instrument this execution is modelled on

stops.name: Temple Mount, the emperor the legend borrows
stops.date_confidence: inferred, and flagged as inference. No source connects Eustace to this pin. Hadrian's 130 decision to found Aelia Capitolina over the ruined platform is attested and dated; the atlas already uses this coordinate in saint_acacius.journey.json as the anchor for a structurally identical undocumented Hadrianic martyrdom, and the same move is made here rather than invent a Roman pin for Eustace.
stops.campa: Hadrian stands on the ruined platform in Jerusalem in 130 and decides to raise a colony and a temple to Jupiter over it, a decision the sources record and date. Two undocumented martyr legends hang on his name: Eustace with his family in the bronze bull, and Acacius, a fellow Fourteen Holy Helper, with the ten thousand on Ararat. Neither leaves a mark in any second-century record. Both are pinned to the emperor's real itinerary, because the emperor is the only part of either story that can be put on a map at all.
sources: saint_acacius.journey.json, stop 'Temple Mount, the emperor the legend names'
suggested_refs: Aelia Capitolina, founded 130, the attested Hadrianic decision used here as an anchor

stops.name: Rome, Sant'Eustachio in a letter of Gregory II
stops.date_confidence: attested as the earliest firm evidence of the cult: a Roman church of Eustace is named in the pontificate of Gregory II (731-741). Coordinate inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the church of Sant'Eustachio'. The month and day default to 01-01; only the pontificate is dated.
stops.campa: A Roman church of Eustace is named in the pontificate of Gregory II, and this is where the dossier stops being literature and begins being evidence. Six hundred years after the year the story assigns itself, there is a building, a name, and a document. Everything before this pin is the Passio: the stag, the crucifix, the shipmaster, the lion, the bull. English Wikipedia calls Eustace a fictitious saint. The church is not fictitious, and it stands as his earliest hard ground.
suggested_refs: The letter of Pope Gregory II naming a Roman church of Eustace

stops.name: Rome, the diaconia of 795
stops.date_confidence: attested for the church: documented as a Roman diaconia in 795 under Leo III (it.wikipedia.org, 'Basilica di Sant'Eustachio'). Not attested for the relics: the porphyry urn under the high altar is said to hold Eustace and his family, but the date of any translation and the authenticity of the contents are not established in anything reachable.
stops.campa: Under Leo III the church enters the records as a diaconia, one of the Roman stations where grain and oil are handed out to the poor of the quarter. The saint whose legend is built on a rich man stripped to nothing is attached, at his first firm address, to a bread queue. The relics said to be his and his family's lie under the high altar in an urn of ancient red porphyry. When they arrived and whether they are his are not settled by anything reachable, and the Italian sources do not pretend otherwise.
suggested_refs: The red porphyry urn beneath the high altar of Sant'Eustachio, Rome

stops.name: Constantinople, the twentieth of September
stops.date_confidence: the feast date is attested in both calendars; the Constantinople coordinate is a placeholder for the Byzantine capital, not a specific shrine, and the 800 date is a bracket for the eighth-to-ninth-century synaxaria rather than a documented event. The oldest Greek passion, BHG 641, is dated by scholars to the fifth to seventh centuries; Latin veneration is attested only from the eighth.
stops.campa: The Byzantine synaxaria carry Eustathios, Theopiste, Agapios and Theopistos on the twentieth of September, the same day the Latin martyrology keeps. East and West divide over most things and do not divide over this date. Churches and relics of Eustathios are claimed in the capital. The oldest surviving text of the whole story is Greek, catalogued BHG 641, dated by scholars anywhere from the fifth century to the seventh, and the Latin West does not venerate him until the eighth.
suggested_refs: BHG 641, the oldest surviving Greek Passio Sancti Eustathii

stops.name: Saint-Denis, Suger's altar of Eustace
stops.date_confidence: attested by Suger (abbot 1122-1151), who records the first relics of Eustace in Europe at an altar of the royal basilica; the relic record is sometimes dated 1140. This corrects an earlier draft of this dossier which put a Carolingian translation here around 800: no Carolingian translation is attested. English Wikipedia adds the caveat that the Eustace venerated at Saint-Denis may have been Eustace of Luxeuil (d. 611).
stops.campa: Abbot Suger, rebuilding the royal abbey north of Paris, records relics of Eustace at one of its altars, the first anywhere in Europe. Denis lies in the crypt of the same church; the memory of Vitus, given away to Corvey in 836, is in the same walls. Suger's note carries a problem he did not know he was making. The Eustace venerated here may be Eustace of Luxeuil, dead in 611, a different man entirely. The relic is attested. Which saint owns it is not.
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint Eustace' (Suger's record; the Luxeuil caveat)
suggested_refs: Suger, De Administratione, on the altars and relics of the rebuilt abbey

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the new choir dedicated
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is inherited from saint_denis.journey.json, whose stop of 11 June 1144 records the consecration of Suger's choir and the placing of Denis under the new high altar. Eustace's presence here is by way of the relics Suger records in the same campaign of works, not by any separate document naming him at the dedication.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of June the new choir is consecrated, the first building in Europe to put pointed arch, rib vault and coloured glass together on purpose, and Denis goes under the new high altar. Louis VII is there and so are the bishops of the realm. The altar with the Eustace relics stands in the same campaign of works. A Roman general whose existence no document supports and a bishop who is said to have carried his own head to this hill share one construction site and one dedication day.
suggested_refs: The consecration of Suger's chevet at Saint-Denis, 11 June 1144

stops.name: Rome, Celestine III takes the church down
stops.date_confidence: attested (it.wikipedia.org, 'Basilica di Sant'Eustachio'): complete rebuilding 1195-1196 under Celestine III with a Romanesque campanile, reconsecrated 1196; Baroque reconstruction across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, principal campaign 1701-1703.
stops.campa: The medieval fabric goes up in 1195 and 1196 under Celestine III, with a Romanesque campanile, and is consecrated in 1196. Then the Tiber floods it and the damp rises through it for five hundred years, until the eighteenth century pulls it down and rebuilds it Baroque: Cesare Corvara first, then Contini, Canevari, Nicola Salvi, Navone. Over the door goes a stag's head with a cross between its antlers. That is the conversion on Monte Guadagnolo, and it is also the arms of the Maffei, who paid for the work.
suggested_refs: The stag's head and cross on the facade of Sant'Eustachio, Maffei arms and conversion emblem at once

stops.name: Chartres, baie 43 in the nave aisle
stops.date_confidence: attested, with two corrections to an earlier draft of this dossier. The Chartres Eustace cycle is baie 43 in the nave aisle, glazed 1205-1215 (fr.wikipedia.org, 'Vitraux de la cathedrale de Chartres'), not the north transept rose: baie 121, the north rose, is c. 1230, dedicated to the Virgin, given by Louis IX and Blanche of Castile. The donor of baie 43 is usually given as the drapers; the 'furriers' attribution is unsupported in the sources checked and is dropped.
stops.campa: In the north aisle of the nave a lancet runs the whole life up its medallions: the hunt, the stag, the baptism, the plague, the ship, the river, the lion, the wolf, the bull. Ordinary Chartres tradespeople pay for it and are painted into the bottom panel at their work. The glass is laid between 1205 and 1215, four centuries before anyone in the church asks whether the man existed, and it treats the story as biography, which is what a window is for. Nobody in this building doubts him.
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, 'Vitraux de la cathedrale de Chartres' (baie 43, 1205-1215)
suggested_refs: Baie 43, the Saint Eustace window, north nave aisle, Chartres Cathedral

stops.name: Genoa, the Golden Legend fixes the story
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Legenda Aurea is compiled c. 1260 by Jacobus de Voragine, Dominican and later archbishop of Genoa. The compilation date is conventional and the year is a bracket, not a document; the month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: Jacobus de Voragine, Dominican and later archbishop of this city, gathers the saints of the year into one book, and the Life of Saint Eustace goes in. The Legenda Aurea becomes the most copied book in Latin Europe after the Bible, and from here every stag and every window in the West is reading this version and no other. Caxton will print it in English in 1483. What survives of Eustace for the next six hundred years survives in the shape a Genoese friar gave it.
sources: The Golden Legend, tr. Caxton (1483), ed. Ellis, Temple Classics (1900)
suggested_refs: Caxton's 1483 English Golden Legend, the vehicle of the story into English

stops.name: Paris, Les Halles: the parish takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested church history (en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint-Eustache, Paris'): chapel to Saint Agnes founded 1213 by the merchant Jean Alais, parish church of Les Halles 1223, renamed for Saint Eustace 1303 on receiving relics from Saint-Denis. The authenticity of those relics is tradition, and they carry the Eustace of Luxeuil ambiguity out of Saint-Denis with them.
stops.campa: A chapel to Saint Agnes, founded by the merchant Jean Alais in 1213, becomes the parish church of the market quarter in 1223 and is renamed for Saint Eustace in 1303, after relics arrive from Saint-Denis. The relics carry the Luxeuil ambiguity out of the abbey and into the largest parish in Paris, and nobody stops to ask. The church rebuilt on this ground in the sixteenth century will baptise Moliere and Richelieu and bury Mirabeau, all of it under the name of a man taken out of a book.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Eustache, Les Halles, Paris, and its 1303 renaming

stops.name: London, Pisanello's huntsman
stops.date_confidence: attested as a painting, c. 1438-1442, National Gallery London NG1436. The commission is unconfirmed: the Gonzaga, Filippo Maria Visconti, Leonello d'Este and Borso d'Este have all been proposed as patrons and none is established. The pin is where the panel hangs, not where it was painted; Pisanello is working in Verona and northern Italy.
stops.campa: Pisanello paints the vision on a small panel: a courtier in a gold tunic and a blue headdress reins in his horse in a dark wood full of hares, bears, deer and dogs, and the stag turns its head with the crucifix in the antlers. He follows the Golden Legend and not the Greek Passio. Who commissioned it is unknown, with the Gonzaga, Filippo Maria Visconti, Leonello and Borso d'Este all proposed and none confirmed. It hangs in the National Gallery as NG1436, a hunting picture a saint has walked into.
suggested_refs: Pisanello, The Vision of Saint Eustace, National Gallery NG1436

stops.name: Liege, the stag walks over to Hubert
stops.date_confidence: attested as a transfer and dated to the fifteenth century, correcting an earlier draft of this dossier which put it around 900. The earliest lives of Hubert, written between 759 and 930, contain no stag and no vision; 'the stag story was only attributed to Saint Hubert in the 15th century' and 'has been appropriated from the legend of Saint Eustace' (en.wikipedia.org, 'Hubertus'). The 1450 date is a mid-century bracket, not a document.
stops.campa: Hubert of Liege, bishop, dead in 727, is given the stag. His own eighth-century and tenth-century lives have no vision in them at all: the crucifix between the antlers is lifted off Eustace and fitted to him in the fifteenth century, and it holds. From then on the hunters of northern Europe pray to Hubert, and the image belongs to whichever of the two the local church prefers. Two men now share one animal, and in most galleries nobody can tell which of them is the one kneeling.
sources: Comparative hagiography of Saint Eustace and Saint Hubert
suggested_refs: Saint-Hubert-en-Ardenne and the fifteenth-century Hubertine stag iconography

stops.name: Nuremberg, Durer cuts the antlers into copper
stops.date_confidence: attested; Durer's 'Saint Eustace' engraving, Bartsch 57, is dated c. 1501. The year is the conventional dating and the month and day default to 01-01. The pin is the canonical Nuremberg coordinate used elsewhere in this atlas.
stops.campa: Durer engraves the plate about 1501: five hounds in five attitudes across the foreground, a castle on the crag, the horse cropping grass, and the huntsman on his knees in front of the stag. It is the largest engraving he ever makes and the one his contemporaries praise most for pure craft. The subject is a saint the Roman church will eventually take off its universal calendar. The print outlives the cult. Most people who know this image today could not put a name to the man in it.
suggested_refs: Durer, Saint Eustace, engraving, Bartsch 57, c. 1501

stops.name: Regensburg, ten around Christopher
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fresco (c. 1320, Dominican church of St Blasius, the oldest surviving group image of the helpers, showing ten and not fourteen). Whether Eustace is among the ten is an open gap: the source does not name the ten. Left open here rather than answered by counting backward from a list that did not yet exist.
stops.campa: In the Dominican church of Saint Blaise, a fellow Fourteen Holy Helper, a fresco of about 1320 puts a group of helper saints around Christopher, another of the fourteen. It is the oldest such group image that survives. There are ten of them, not fourteen, and the source does not name which ten. Whether Eustace is already standing in that fresco, or joins later when the Franconian dioceses fix the list, is a question left open here because the evidence leaves it open.
suggested_refs: The c. 1320 Nothelfer fresco, Dominikanerkirche St. Blasius, Regensburg

stops.name: Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fixed list by about 1400 across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from saint_acacius, saint_blaise, saint_cyriacus, saint_denis and catorce_santos_ayudantes, all of which carry this pin and quote this list verbatim.
stops.campa: By about 1400 the Franconian sequence is closed and repeated without variation across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Eustace stands ninth, between Erasmus and George. Acacius, Blaise, Cyriacus and Denis all quote this list word for word in their own files here, and each already carries this pin. He is named by position in four journeys before he has one of his own.
suggested_refs: The closed Franconian sequence of the Vierzehn Nothelfer, c. 1400

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, fourteen children in red and white
stops.date_confidence: attested as an apparition tradition, 1445-1446, at the Langheim monastery lands. Eustace is one of the fourteen counted in afterward from the Franconian list, not one named by the children; the sources record no individual naming. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from saint_barbara, san_vito, giles, saint_acacius and catorce_santos_ayudantes.
stops.campa: A shepherd of the Langheim monastery sees a child in a field where no child should be, and then sees fourteen of them, in red and white, who say they are the fourteen helpers and ask for a chapel on that spot. The apparitions run through 1445 and 1446 and the chapel is built. Eustace is one of the fourteen counted in from the Franconian list, not one the children name. Barbara, Vitus, Giles and Acacius, fellow helpers, already stand on this exact coordinate. Eustace makes five.
suggested_refs: The 1445-1446 shepherd apparitions on the Langheim lands at Vierzehnheiligen

stops.name: Heilsbronn Minster, the altar of the assembled fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the altar (1498, Heilsbronn Minster, showing the fourteen assembled; by this point the devotion has spread to Sweden, Hungary and Italy). The catorce file does not name Eustace individually at this stop; his presence is by set membership, and which carved figure he is cannot be established from the sources reached.
stops.campa: The Nothelfer altar at Heilsbronn shows the fourteen assembled in one frame, and by this date the devotion has run out of Franconia into Sweden, Hungary and Italy. Eustace is in the panel by list membership. The surviving descriptions do not name the figures one by one, so which carved man is the general with the stag cannot be said from anything reachable. He is present the way a name in a litany is present, which is how he has been present since Nuremberg closed the count a century before.
suggested_refs: The 1498 Nothelfer altar, Heilsbronn Minster, Middle Franconia

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, Neumann's basilica consecrated
stops.date_confidence: attested: cornerstone 1743, consecration 1772, Balthasar Neumann architect, the plan bent around an altar that could not be moved because it marked the apparition spot. Coordinate and both dates inherited from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json and saint_acacius.journey.json, where the same architectural fact is already narrated.
stops.campa: Balthasar Neumann lays the cornerstone in 1743 and the church is consecrated in 1772, built around an altar that could not be moved because it stood where the shepherd saw the children. Neumann solves the problem by making that altar the centre of an oval the whole building bends around. Eustace has his niche on the Gnadenaltar with the other thirteen: a Roman general in stucco holding a stag's head, in Upper Franconia, sixteen centuries and two thousand kilometres from anything a document can support.
suggested_refs: The Gnadenaltar of the Vierzehnheiligen basilica, Balthasar Neumann, consecrated 1772

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the ranked rows
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1780 Nothelferaltar of Peter Vambach in the Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main, carving the fourteen in ranked rows, each identified by attribute. The catorce file calls this the one object in the corpus that three separate journeys inherited without changing a digit; Eustace takes the same coordinate as a fourth.
stops.campa: Peter Vambach carves the fourteen into ranked rows for the Anna-Kapelle in 1780, each one identified by what he carries, Barbara and Catherine and Vitus among them. Eustace stands in the same rows and takes the same pin, a fourth traveller arriving at a single wooden altar in a small town on the Main. Saints carved together at the same altar are counted together and end up located together.
suggested_refs: Peter Vambach's Nothelferaltar of 1780, Anna-Kapelle, Obernburg am Main

stops.name: Sint Eustatius, the island in the Dutch Caribbean
stops.date_confidence: attested as a name in continuous official use; the sources reached date the naming only to the seventeenth century, so the year here is the Dutch settlement of 1636 and the month and day are defaults. No source found records the act of naming or who performed it.
stops.campa: A volcanic island of eight square miles in the Leeward Antilles carries his name and keeps it. The Dutch take it in 1636 and it becomes the busiest free port in the Caribbean, the Golden Rock, the first foreign government to salute the flag of the United States. It is now a special municipality of the Netherlands and is still called Sint Eustatius. A saint the Roman church would eventually decline to vouch for is the legal name of a jurisdiction, in force, today.
suggested_refs: Fort Oranje, Sint Eustatius, and the 1776 salute to the Andrew Doria

stops.name: Saint-Eustache, the parish on the Riviere du Chene
stops.date_confidence: attested: Saint-Eustache, Quebec, founded 1770, incorporated 1835 (en.wikipedia.org, 'Saint-Eustache, Quebec'). Two corrections to an earlier draft of this dossier: the founding year is 1770, not 1780, and there is no Roman Catholic Diocese of Saint-Eustache. No such see exists; the town lies in the Diocese of Saint-Jerome-Mont-Laurier. The diocese claim is withdrawn.
stops.campa: A parish is founded in 1770 on the Riviere du Chene north-west of Montreal and takes the name. It is incorporated as a town in 1835, and two years after that the church is shelled with British artillery in the Patriote rebellion, the walls still carrying the marks. The name travels the way names travel, on parish registers and by whoever named the seigneury, with no relics, no legend, and nobody in the village having read the Passio. Most of the cult's reach consists of exactly this.
sources: Diocesan and toponymic records for Saint-Eustache, Quebec
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Eustache, Quebec, and the shot marks of 14 December 1837

stops.name: Rome, four names come off the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1969 revision of the General Roman Calendar (Calendarium Romanum, Consilium under Paul VI) removes the universal feasts of Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria, Christopher and Margaret of Antioch. Contradiction in the pool, recorded not resolved: one line of the research states that Eustace's own feast is removed in 1969 for the same reason, while the Fourteen Helpers file counts him among the ten left untouched. The atlas follows the arithmetic of the Fourteen file and flags the disagreement here.
stops.campa: The revised General Roman Calendar drops Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria, Christopher and Margaret of Antioch, fellow Fourteen Holy Helpers, from the universal feasts on the ground that their acts are legendary. Eustace's acts are legendary too. Whether the reform touches him is a point on which the consulted sources disagree, and the disagreement is left standing: he is counted among the ten survivors elsewhere in the record. The Eastern churches keep Eustathios, Theopiste, Agapios and Theopistos on the twentieth of September with no revision at all.
sources: Calendarium Romanum, 1969 reform (Consilium under Paul VI)
